summary: Defines where the RIPng protocol is applicable within the Internet, as required by the routing protocol criteria of the time. It is an informational applicability statement.

plainLanguage.summary: RIPng adapts the simple RIP-2 routing protocol for IPv6. This memo explains where it may fit and why larger or more complex networks need another approach.

subtitle: Where the RFC says the RIPng routing protocol fits in IPv6 networks.

tldr.problem: The memo explains the intended place for RIPng, the IPv6 adaptation of RIP-2, and its limits.
tldr.mechanism: It describes IPv6 prefixes, next-hop behavior, larger update packets, and a maximum metric of 15, with 16 meaning unreachable.
tldr.outcome: The RFC presents RIPng as a simple option for moderate networks, not as a replacement for OSPFng in large or complex networks.

today: RFC 2081 is an Informational applicability statement. The unit metadata lists no later update or replacement.

sections.title: The Role of RIPng
sections.content:
RFC 2081 is an applicability statement for RIPng, whose protocol description is in RFC 2080. The memo says RIPng serves a similar niche in IPv6 to RIP-2 in IPv4.

It is not intended to replace OSPFng in large autonomous systems. The distance-vector design has limits on network diameter and complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: RIPng is intended for networks where a simple routing protocol is enough. The memo says it is not meant for large, complex systems that need OSPFng.

sections.title: Changes for IPv6
sections.content:
The RFC describes a 128-bit address field and an 8-bit prefix-length field, replacing RIP-2's 32-bit address and subnet-mask field. The route tag is retained, and the next-hop field is removed while its functionality is preserved.

The maximum metric remains 15; 16 means infinity, or unreachable. Authentication is removed, which the memo says is safe because IPv6 has built-in security.
sections.plainLanguage: RIPng carries IPv6 prefixes instead of IPv4 addresses and masks. It keeps the route limit of 15 hops, with 16 meaning unreachable.

sections.title: Updates and Network Complexity
sections.content:
RIPng routing packets are not limited to an arbitrary fixed size in this description. Their size depends on the media MTU after preceding headers, which can let an update contain more routes and reduce the number of packets sent.

The memo says RIPng can support moderate-complexity networks, especially those without many multi-hop loops. It also describes incremental route changes as useful when topologies change often.
sections.plainLanguage: A larger update can carry more routes at once. The memo sees RIPng as a fit for moderate networks, not ones with many routing loops.

references.text: Malkin, G., "RIPng Protocol Description", RFC 2080, January 1997.
Rekhter, Y., and T. Li, "RIP-2 Protocol Applicability Statement", RFC 1723, November 1994.
